title: What Is Slotted Track? Avoid Costly Wall Problems 2026
description: A practical, engineer-backed guide to slotted deflection track—how it works, where to use it, and field-proven installation steps.
html:
Last updated: October 2026

Key takeaway:

Slotted track is a head-of-wall framing track that lets steel studs accommodate vertical movement in the structure without transferring that movement into drywall finishes. The track’s elongated slots allow the approved fasteners to move while the partition remains aligned, but the slot length, stud gap, fasteners, firestop, and ceiling interface must all match the project’s movement requirement.

By Navjot Dass • Dass Metal Products
Last updated: October 26, 2026

What should you know about slotted track first?

Slotted track, also called slotted deflection track or slotted leg track, is installed at the top of a non-load-bearing steel stud wall. It is used where the slab, deck, roof structure, or perimeter construction above the wall may move vertically relative to the partition below. Instead of locking the stud tops rigidly to the structure, the detail allows controlled movement at the head-of-wall joint.

This matters because a finished partition cannot safely absorb every movement that a building experiences. Floor deflection, wind drift, seismic movement, construction loading, and temperature-related movement can place stress on gypsum board, joint compound, doors, ceilings, and adjacent finishes. A correctly detailed slotted track helps keep that movement at the joint rather than forcing it into the wall finish.

  • Use it where drawings or engineering documents identify head-of-wall movement.
  • Confirm the required travel before selecting the profile or ordering material.
  • Keep fasteners, sealants, firestop, ceilings, and services from defeating the movement detail.
  • Inspect the assembly before boarding so the studs can move as designed.

For a broader explanation of movement accommodation, see this deflection track overview. The product decision should still be based on the project drawings, structural movement calculations, applicable specifications, and the selected fire- or sound-rated assembly.

What is slotted track?

Slotted track is a cold-formed steel U-shaped track with vertical slots in its legs. Steel studs are fitted into the track at the head of a wall, and the specified fasteners pass through the slots. When the structure above moves vertically, the fasteners can travel within the slots instead of forcing the stud and finished wall to move rigidly with it.

The track does not make a wall independent of the building, and it does not replace structural engineering. It creates a controlled interface for a particular movement direction and range. The designer must identify the expected movement, the wall system, the track profile, the fastener arrangement, and the compatible joint treatment together.

Where is it used?

Common locations include interior partitions below concrete slabs or steel decks, perimeter walls below curtain-wall or spandrel conditions, corridor heads, shaft-wall intersections, and walls beneath long-span framing. It may also be appropriate where wind or seismic drift creates relative movement, subject to the project’s design and the selected assembly listing.

Slotted track is generally a head-of-wall product. Standard, non-slotted track may remain appropriate at a fixed bottom-of-wall condition or another location where the drawings do not require movement. Do not substitute one for the other based only on appearance or availability.

For additional terminology and diagrams, compare this slotted deflection track guide with the product data required for the specific wall assembly.

Why does slotted track matter?

A building’s primary structure and its interior partitions do not always move at the same rate. A floor may deflect as occupants and equipment load it, while a roof or deck may move as construction loads change. If a partition is rigidly fastened at the head, that relative movement can appear as cracked joints, displaced corner beads, buckled studs, damaged sealant, or doors that no longer operate smoothly.

Slotted track gives the detail a defined place to accommodate movement. It can reduce the likelihood that movement will be concentrated in the gypsum finish, but only when the complete assembly remains free to move. A rigid screw installation, an oversized bead of hardened sealant, a ceiling connection, or a service support can create a bridge that transfers the same stress the track was intended to manage.

What problems can the detail help prevent?

  • Finish cracking: Movement is less likely to be forced into taped joints and corner finishes when the head detail is free to travel.
  • Stud binding: Proper clearance and fastener placement help prevent the studs from being trapped against the structure.
  • Misalignment: A coordinated detail helps the wall remain plumb while the structure moves within the design envelope.
  • Trade rework: Early coordination reduces the chance that firestop, ceilings, ducts, or conduits will later block movement.

These benefits are not automatic. The specified movement must be transferred into the drawings, shop details, material selection, installation instructions, and inspection checklist. A product cannot compensate for a missing movement allowance or an incompatible rated joint system.

How does slotted deflection track work?

The elongated vertical slots form a travel path for the approved fasteners. The track is attached to the structure above, while the stud is positioned within the track with the designed clearance at its top. As relative vertical movement occurs, the fastener can slide in the slot rather than clamping the stud to a fixed point.

The direction of movement is important. A typical slotted head-of-wall detail is intended to accommodate vertical movement; it is not a universal solution for every horizontal or lateral condition. Wind and seismic requirements may require additional engineering, clips, bracing, or a tested system. Follow the drawings and the manufacturer’s installation requirements rather than assuming that a slotted profile handles all movement modes.

What are the main components?

  • Slotted track: The selected profile must provide the required leg height, gauge, coating, slot geometry, and movement capacity.
  • Steel studs: Stud size and gauge must match the wall design. Studs are cut to preserve the required head clearance.
  • Fasteners: Use the type, location, and spacing identified by the product data, wall design, or tested assembly. The fastener must be able to travel in the slot.
  • Joint materials: Firestop, acoustical sealant, insulation, and other materials must be compatible with the expected movement.
  • Adjacent construction: Ceilings, ducts, pipes, conduits, and supports must not create an unintended rigid connection.

Track geometry, leg height, and related steel framing terminology are covered in this metal stud track guide. Those basics are useful when reviewing a submittal, but the project specification remains the controlling source for the final selection.

How should you choose a slotted track profile?

Start with the required movement, then check the wall height, stud gauge, track leg height, finish tolerances, fire rating, acoustic objective, and available clearance. The movement requirement should not be inferred from a generic product description. Architectural and structural documents may state the expected travel directly, or the design team may need to calculate it.

Standard slotted deflection track

Standard slotted track is commonly considered for straight interior and exterior framing conditions where the specified movement fits the product’s published capacity. Review slot length, slot width, leg dimensions, material thickness, corrosion protection, and approved fasteners before ordering. Product information for Dass Metal’s slotted deflection track can support that review, but the project team must confirm compatibility with the intended assembly.

Deep-leg or taller track

A deeper profile may provide additional engagement and layout tolerance for taller walls or conditions with a larger movement envelope. It is not automatically a higher-capacity solution: the wall design, stud position, ceiling clearance, slot travel, and tested head-of-wall system still have to work together. Review the available standard track options when comparing leg dimensions and adjacent interfaces.

Curved track for radiused walls

Radiused corridors, feature walls, and curved office fronts may need a track that follows the wall geometry while retaining the required movement detail. A curved product such as U-Flex track should be coordinated with the stud layout, ceiling, drywall, and rated joint requirements. Curvature does not remove the need to verify movement capacity.

How is slotted track installed?

Installation begins with the design movement, not with the track shipment. The framing crew should have the approved head-of-wall detail, product information, fastener requirements, and coordinated fire and acoustic details available before layout. The following sequence is a practical field framework; the project documents and product instructions govern where they differ.

  1. Confirm the movement: Identify the required vertical travel, direction, joint type, and any minimum or maximum clearance shown on the drawings.
  2. Set out the track: Establish the wall line and anchor the track to the supporting structure with the specified fasteners. Keep the slots in the intended orientation and clear of debris.
  3. Cut the studs: Cut studs so the designed head gap remains available. Do not pack the gap with rigid material or allow the stud to bear hard against the structure.
  4. Place and fasten the studs: Position the studs in the track and install fasteners through the slots using the approved location and spacing. Do not substitute a rigid connection without design approval.
  5. Coordinate the joint: Install only compatible firestop, acoustical sealant, insulation, and other materials. Each layer must allow the specified movement.
  6. Inspect before boarding: Check slot orientation, head clearance, fastener placement, track anchorage, stud alignment, and unobstructed travel before gypsum board conceals the detail.

What installation errors are most common?

  • Overdriving fasteners: Excessive tightening can deform the track or restrict sliding. Use the specified installation method and check the fastener’s ability to move.
  • Using the wrong slot or screw location: A fastener outside the intended travel path can turn a sliding connection into a fixed one.
  • Blocking the head gap: Mortar, concrete splatter, scraps, insulation, or rigid sealant can consume the movement allowance.
  • Bridging with other trades: A duct support, ceiling channel, conduit, sprinkler component, or framing clip can lock the wall to the structure.
  • Assuming all firestop is interchangeable: Rated joints must use a system that is listed or specified for the substrate, joint size, movement, and required rating.

Adjacent framing details may require other profiles or transitions. For example, the bottom plate framing guide addresses a different part of the wall and should not be treated as a substitute for a head-of-wall movement detail.

What belongs in the specification and submittal?

A useful specification tells the contractor more than “provide slotted track.” It identifies the location, movement requirement, material properties, attachment method, and coordination requirements. A complete submittal then demonstrates that the proposed product and assembly meet those instructions.

Specification items to identify

  • Required vertical movement and the basis for that movement.
  • Wall type, stud size, gauge, height, and loading condition.
  • Track leg height, base metal thickness, coating, slot dimensions, and published travel.
  • Track anchorage, stud fasteners, spacing, and any restrictions on fastening through the slots.
  • Required head gap, installation tolerances, and inspection expectations.
  • Fire-resistance, smoke, acoustic, thermal, or air-sealing requirements.
  • Coordination requirements for ceilings, curtain wall, MEP penetrations, and adjacent partitions.

Submittal questions for review

  • Does the product data state a movement capacity equal to or greater than the project requirement?
  • Are the proposed track dimensions compatible with the studs, finishes, ceiling, and available space?
  • Do the fasteners and spacing match the product data and the wall design?
  • Does the firestop system accommodate the same joint width and movement?
  • Are installation details clear enough for the framing and finishing crews to follow?
  • Are substitutions identified rather than silently exchanged for standard track?

For adjacent framing conditions, the L track product information may help with interface discussions, but it does not establish that an L profile is suitable for a moving head-of-wall joint.

How do fire, acoustics, ceilings, and MEP affect the detail?

The slotted track is only one part of a head-of-wall assembly. A fire-rated joint, for example, must be selected as a compatible tested or listed system rather than assembled from unrelated materials. The joint’s movement rating, substrates, width, depth, and installation method all matter.

Firestopping

Confirm that the selected firestop system is intended for the joint and movement range shown in the documents. A rigid or incorrectly sized material can restrict the track or leave the joint unprotected. Record the approved system in the submittal and inspect it before concealment.

Acoustic control

Acoustical sealant and insulation should close the intended gaps without creating an unintended rigid bridge. Slotted track manages structural movement; it does not by itself establish an STC rating. The full wall, head joint, penetrations, doors, ceilings, and adjacent construction determine acoustic performance.

Ceilings and services

Floating or otherwise compatible ceiling interfaces may be needed where the partition head must move independently. Ducts, pipes, conduits, sprinkler systems, cable trays, and supports should be reviewed at coordination meetings so they do not pin the wall to the structure. Where services cross a movement joint, use the flexible or slip detail required by the design.

Rated shaft returns and similar intersections require additional care. Review this shaft wall framing guide for related framing considerations, then confirm the exact intersection with the project’s rated assembly and design team.

Availability and timing should be confirmed for the actual project rather than assumed from a general product description.

Local project conditions still require project-specific design. Vaughan location, Ontario climate, or a cross-border delivery route does not determine the movement capacity. The structural documents, wall design, product data, and applicable code or tested assembly do.

How do you inspect and troubleshoot slotted track?

Inspect the detail before insulation and board hide the connection. Start at representative locations and include corners, intersections, transitions, rated joints, ceiling interfaces, and areas crowded by services. Photograph deviations and resolve them through the responsible trade or design professional before proceeding.

Preboard inspection checklist

  • Track is the specified profile, gauge, coating, and orientation.
  • Anchors are installed into the correct supporting structure and are not damaged or loose.
  • Stud tops have the required clearance and are not bearing hard against the deck or slab.
  • Fasteners are in the intended slots, use the approved type, and are not overdriven.
  • Slots and the movement path are free from concrete, screws, wire, sealant, and debris.
  • Firestop, acoustical materials, ceilings, and services do not bridge the joint.
  • The wall is plumb and the head detail corresponds with the approved drawings.

Symptoms and likely checks

If cracks appear at the ceiling line, doors become difficult to operate, or the wall makes noise during movement, inspect for a blocked slot, missing head clearance, rigid sealant, incorrect fasteners, or a trade connection that has fixed the partition to the structure. Also verify that the required movement was not greater than the selected product’s published capacity.

Do not solve a suspected movement problem by simply cutting away material or loosening fasteners without authorization. Document the condition, compare it with the approved detail, and involve the framing manufacturer, contractor, architect, engineer, or firestop specialist as appropriate.

Frequently asked questions about slotted track

Where should slotted track be used?

Use it at head-of-wall conditions where the design anticipates relative vertical movement between the structure and a steel stud partition. Typical locations include walls below slabs or decks, perimeter walls, long-span framing, and selected rated or shaft intersections. The drawings and specifications should confirm the location and required travel.

How much movement can slotted track accommodate?

Capacity depends on the specific profile, slot geometry, installation, and tested or published product data. Some referenced slotted track systems are designed for total vertical movement of 1 1/2 inches, but that value must not be applied to every product or project. Select a track whose documented capacity meets the movement stated by the design team, and coordinate the same travel with firestop and adjacent construction.

Can standard track be used at a moving head-of-wall?

Standard non-slotted track should not be used where the design requires movement unless the design professional specifically approves a different detail. Because it lacks the intended travel path, it can rigidly connect the studs to the structure and transfer movement into the finishes. Use the specified slotted or other engineered deflection system instead.

Does slotted track replace resilient channel?

No. Slotted track accommodates structural movement at the head of the wall, while resilient channel is used as part of an acoustic decoupling strategy. A partition may require one, both, or neither depending on its movement, fire, sound, and finish requirements. Treat them as separate design decisions and coordinate their interfaces.
